_format.description: Ujednolicony format eksportu danych ze stron NASA (science.nasa.gov i pokrewnych). Ten sam schemat stosuj do każdej kolejnej strony misji/pojazdu, aby wszystkie wpisy były spójne i mogły być łączone w jedną bazę.
conventions: Klucze zawsze obecne; brak danych = null (nigdy nie usuwaj klucza), brak pozycji = pusta lista [].
Daty: 'date' zawsze w ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD), 'date_raw' zachowuje oryginalny zapis ze strony.
Wszystkie URL-e bezwzględne (https://...), bez parametrów śledzących gdzie to możliwe.
Każdy zasób medialny jest obiektem z minimalnym zestawem pól: url + typ + context (skąd pochodzi na stronie).
Treść artykułu w polach 'markdown': nagłówki '##'/'###', listy '-', listy numerowane '1.', pogrubienia '**'. Układ = kolejność sekcji ze strony źródłowej.
Treść zachowywana w języku źródła (pole source.language); nie tłumaczyć przy ekstrakcji.
Pola 'id' zewnętrznych systemów (np. PIA##### z Photojournal, identyfikatory YouTube, numery modeli 3D) zapisuj w dedykowanych polach *_id, jeśli są znane.
Weryfikuj dostępność URL-i (HTTP 200) przed zapisem; martwy link oznaczaj w polu 'status'.

Two solar panels, about 7 feet (2.2 meters) each in diameter
2 color cameras (1 is a "fisheye"); image size 1,024 pixels by 1,024 pixels
3 (a seismometer, heat probe, and a radio science experiment)
To place SEIS, the seismometer, and HP3, the Heat Flow and Physical Properties Package, on the surface of Mars
Four (side-to-side and up-and-down at the shoulder, plus bending at the elbow and wrist joints) with four motors

SEIS — Seismic Experiment for Interior Structure (seismometer); HP3 — Heat Flow and Physical Properties Package (heat probe / "mole"); RISE — Rotation and Interior Structure Experiment (radio science)
IDC — Instrument Deployment Camera (on the arm; 45-degree field of view, full color); ICC — Instrument Context Camera (below the deck edge; 120-degree "fisheye" field of view)

article.title: InSight Lander
article.lead: InSight Lander was the first outer space robotic explorer to study in-depth the inner space of Mars: its crust, mantle, and core.

sections.heading: Featured Story: NASA Marsquake Data Reveals Lumpy Nature of Red Planet’s Interior
sections.markdown:
Rocky material that impacted Mars lies scattered in giant lumps throughout the planet’s mantle, offering clues about Mars’ interior…

[Read the Story](https://www.nasa.gov/missions/insight/nasa-marsquake-data-reveals-lumpy-nature-of-red-planets-interior/)

sections.heading: Meet InSight
sections.markdown:
The lander was built on the proven design of NASA's [Mars Phoenix lander](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/phoenix/). InSight's robotic arm was over 5 feet 9 inches (1.8 meters) long. It lifted a seismometer and heat flow probe from the deck and placed them on the surface.

[Learn More About the Spacecraft](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/insight/spacecraft/)

sections.heading: Wind Sounds on Mars
sections.markdown:
InSight sensors captured a haunting low rumble caused by vibrations from the Martian wind, estimated to be blowing at 10 to 15 mph (5 to 7 meters a second) on Dec. 1, 2018. The winds were consistent with the direction of dust devil streaks in the landing area, which were observed from orbit.

**Audio/Video:** [Sounds of Mars: NASA’s InSight Senses Martian Wind (YouTube)](https://youtu.be/yT50Q_Zbf3s)

sections.heading: Key Dates
sections.markdown:
- **Launched:** May 5, 2018 (4:05 a.m. PT / 7:05 a.m. ET)
- **Launch Vehicle:** Atlas V-401
- **Launch Location:** Vandenberg Air Force Base, California
- **Landed:** Nov. 26, 2018, at 11:52:59 a.m. PT (2:52:59 p.m. ET)
- **Landing Site:** Elysium Planitia, Mars
- **End of Mission:** Dec. 15, 2022

sections.heading: Read More
sections.markdown:
- **Objective** — The InSight mission had two major goals, each with several science investigations, designed to help uncover the process that shaped all of the rocky planets in the inner solar system. [Explore](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/insight/science/)
- **Science** — InSight studied the deep interior of Mars and was designed to take the planet's vital signs: its pulse, temperature, and reflexes. [Explore](https://go.nasa.gov/3X2YxNh)

sections.heading: Landing Site: Elysium Planitia
sections.markdown:
InSight landed near Mars' equator on the western side of a flat, smooth plain called Elysium Planitia. Elysium Planitia was selected not for its surface features, but for safety considerations. InSight's purpose was to study the interior of Mars, not the surface. Thus, in the selection of a landing site, what's on the surface mattered less than for previous rover missions focused on the geology.

Planitia is Latin for a flat surface, geometric plane, or flatness or a plain. Elysium is from the ancient Greek name for an afterlife paradise, usually referred to in English as the Elysian Fields. The landing site lies in the western portion of Elysium Planitia, centered at about 4.5 degrees north latitude and 135.9 degrees east longitude. This is just 373 miles (600 kilometers) from Curiosity’s landing site, Gale Crater.

*Image: The red dot marks the final landing location of NASA's InSight lander in this annotated image of the surface of Mars, taken by the THEMIS camera on NASA's 2001 Mars Odyssey orbiter in 2015. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/ASU*

sections.heading: Mars Cube One: The First Interplanetary CubeSats
sections.markdown:
The rocket that launched InSight also launched a separate NASA technology experiment: two mini-spacecraft called Mars Cube One, or MarCO. These briefcase-sized CubeSats flew on their own path to Mars behind InSight.

[Learn More](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/marco/)
